title: Ecosystem collapse

definition.text: The loss of an ecosystem's defining features and the services it provided once destabilising pressures push it past a critical threshold.

facts.text: Collapse does not mean all life disappears; the original ecosystem is replaced by a novel one with greatly altered structure and function.
It has been called an analogue of species extinction and is usually irreversible; any recovery is slow and needs active intervention.
Human drivers include introducing species, overexploitation, pollution, climate change and habitat destruction or fragmentation.
Collapse can occur when an ecosystem shrinks below a minimum viable size or loses key biotic processes.
Even at 1.5 °C of warming, only 0.2% of the world's coral reefs could withstand marine heatwaves, against 84% now.
Under a high-emissions scenario, tropical ocean ecosystems could face abrupt disruption before 2030, with tropical forests and polar regions following by 2050.
Little is known yet about effective ways to conserve or reverse collapsing ecosystems.

related: Tipping points in the climate system
notes: The dossier's Definition line (S:acce03c90953) defines 'ecosystem', not collapse; the definition uses lead sentences instead.

definition.text: Documented cases in which ecosystems collapsed through overuse, climate shocks or introduced species.

facts.text: Easter Island's palm-dominated forests collapsed from overexploitation, climate change and introduced rats.
The Aral Sea shrank after its feeder rivers were diverted for irrigation, falling to 10% of its original size by 1997.
Overfishing reduced Grand Banks cod to 1% of historical levels in the early 1990s.
In the northern Benguela upwelling, overfishing and climate events turned a sardine-dominated ecosystem into one dominated by jellyfish and goby.

definition.text: Tools such as risk assessment protocols and simulation models that estimate how close ecosystems are to collapse.

facts.text: The IUCN Red List of Ecosystems is a global standard that works even where data are scarce.
It uses Collapsed as the end-point category, with Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered defined by the risk of collapse.
Because it compares systems to a criteria list, it is often paired with simulation models covering dynamics, future threats and social links.

title: Ecosystem health

definition.text: A metaphor for the overall condition of an ecosystem.

facts.text: Fire, drought, invasive species, climate change, mining, fishing, farming and logging can all change ecosystem condition.
There is no universal benchmark; judgements depend on the metrics chosen and the goals of society.
Supporters value it as a simple communication tool, while critics call it a value-laden idea passed off as science.
Aldo Leopold spoke of land health and land sickness; the health metaphor dates back at least to the early 1800s.
The Great Lakes Basin uses a suite of 80 lake health indicators, including native fish, phosphorus and toxic chemicals.
A healthy state is hard to pin down because species in an ecosystem reshuffle over time.
Proposed neutral alternatives include ecosystem status, ecosystem prognosis and ecosystem sustainability.

contested_note: Critics argue ecosystem health is a value judgement rather than a scientific measure.

definition.text: The difference between indicators used to describe trends scientifically and those used to rank conditions as good or bad for policy.

facts.text: An indicator is a measured variable used to infer trends in something unmeasured; rising chlorophyll-a in a lake may signal eutrophication.
The same chlorophyll level may be judged healthy in a natural wetland and unhealthy in a human-impacted one.
Critics say mixing the two implies values can be measured objectively, and urge keeping them separate.

title: Health paradox
article: Ecosystem health#Relationship to human health: the health paradox

definition.text: The trade-off in which human health has often improved by sacrificing the health of wild ecosystems.

facts.text: Examples include damming valleys, draining mosquito-bearing wetlands, diverting water for irrigation and converting wilderness to farmland.
The utilitarian view treats human well-being as a test of ecosystem health; the protectionist view sees humans as an invasive species.
Utilitarians argue unhealthy ecosystems bring more disease, fires, floods, crop failures and fishery collapse.

contested_note: Conservationists and resource managers are split over whether to scale back or embrace human domination of the biosphere.
